title: Dare I say “marked safe from Tommy Kail’s Warriors”? #broadway #music...
transcript: By now you've probably heard the announcement that Lin-Manuel Miranda and Eisa Davis's new musical, Warriors, is coming to Broadway. But there is one hugely important piece of this that I haven't heard anyone really talk about at all, even when the workshop was announced a few months ago, and that is the co-director, Jenny koons. If you haven't heard of Jenny koons, she is a very experienced director. She's done a lot of work regionally. She's done some stuff in New York off Broadway as well. In fact, she was the director of one of my favorite recent plays. Regretfully so, the birds are. Later that year I also saw a show she directed at Soho Rep called The Whitney Album. Both of which I will say were very small scale and very intimate and a little bit off kilter and weird in a way that I wouldn't necessarily associate with warriors. Not that she doesn't have experience with large scale productions, but this is, I think, her first foray into the sort of development of a big new Broadway musical. Based on the work of hers that I've seen, I wouldn't necessarily have thought of her for a project like Warriors, but there's also something kind of exciting about that. I posted a video, I think, last week about how many directors there are who currently have two shows running on Broadway at the same time. And a lot of people were very quick to point out And all of the directors I named were white men. I think it is very rare for an Asian woman to get a chance to direct a new Broadway musical. I honestly can't think of the last time it's happened, but I would love to hear if someone knows off hand. But even beyond that element of it, just like new people in general, when I posted my review of the Warriors album a couple years ago, whenever it came out, I really loved it. But the one thing I said was, god, I hope they managed to keep this feeling kind of weird and gritty. I really hope when it gets translated to the stage that it doesn't undergo the same kind of flattening and homogenization of style and tone that so many Broadway musicals go through, especially when it's, like, using genre music. And so to get the directorial perspective of someone who's not from that world of big, sleek Broadway musicals is very exciting to me. And just the simple fact that she's been working in the industry for a while and hasn't gotten this sort of high profile spotlight gig yet
